name: Daria Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Daria. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything is confidential. What does a normal day on your farm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Pavel and I bought Willow Bank Farm three years ago: seventy hectares, three hundred ewes, some barley and a small apple orchard. I'm out at six checking the sheep, then it's fencing, moving the flock, or the barley, depending on the month. In the evenings I do the accounts and the online lamb box orders. Before this I ran parcel schedules at a warehouse for fourteen years, so I'm very new at the actual farming.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alan, the old farmer next door, mostly. He laughs at me but he always comes when I ring. And I use AI every day: I ask it about foot rot, it plans the grazing rotation, it drafts the lamb box emails. Alan thinks that's cheating, but it's kept two ewes alive this spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things with money and family?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We sold our house in town to buy the farm, so most of our money is the land itself, plus a farm loan and some savings. Pavel's a land surveyor, three days a week, which steadies things. Anja's twelve and Filip's nine and they love it here. Last year the farm made a small loss, wet August, flattened barley, cheap lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are good but they were never going to farm for us. I'd post something in the new farmers' group about which apps are actually worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worries don't change. AI writing my emails doesn't help when lamb prices drop and the barley lies flat after a wet August. We can afford a bad year, we've got the land and savings, but two more would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and grow the lamb box scheme, because selling direct pays twice what the market does. I'd keep using AI for the paperwork and grazing. And I'd plant another row of apple trees for a cider sideline Pavel keeps talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, the way I always am about money in autumn. Not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two more bad years mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use up the savings and have to talk about selling the bottom twenty hectares to Alan. I'd hate that. It's the best grazing we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Alan say about your AI use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alan says his father managed without a phone. I tell him his father had five sons to help. We're even.

think: AI doesn't help with **lamb prices** or barley flattened by a wet August.
We can afford one **bad year**, but two more would hurt.
do: **Grow** the lamb box scheme, which pays twice the market rate.
**Keep** using AI for paperwork and grazing plans.
**Plant** another row of apple trees for cider.

steps.text: Grow the online lamb box scheme to more customers
Keep using AI to plan grazing and do the accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers should love this bit, because it takes the jobs we hate. Forms, ordering, accounts. I'd tell the new farmers' group to get on it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news. I'd let a computer do every subsidy form on Willow Bank Farm and spend the saved hours with my sheep. Pavel's surveying reports would change, but he's out on sites half the time, so I think he's all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the subsidy claims, feed ordering and lamb box marketing fully to AI tools in the first few months. I'd buy a drone to count and check the flock on the far hill. And I'd use the time saved to do a proper lambing course with Alan's vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the saved hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the sheep properly. I still can't body-condition score a ewe as fast as Alan, he just runs his hand down her back. That's the gap I want to close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any downside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone gets good at marketing with AI, my lamb boxes aren't special any more. I'd need to find another edge, maybe the orchard.

**Book** a lambing course with Alan's vet.

steps.text: Hand subsidy claims and feed ordering to AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms need help to buy robots together, or the big operators win everything. I'd push the farmers' group to set up a shared machinery scheme. I'd be practical about it, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 part is fine for me, I'm already using it. But Pavel's surveying reports could be AI work by then, and that's our steady money. And 2031 is the real threat: a small farm like mine can't buy the robot in 2031, but the big farm down the road can, and then sell lamb cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sell the bottom twenty hectares to Alan to clear the farm loan, so we're lean and debt-free. I'd put money into a shared robot scheme with three neighbours. Pavel would move into site inspections, the outdoor part AI can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but busy. I'd be on the phone every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel selling land to Alan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted, honestly, that's the best grazing. But Alan would let me rent it back, he's said so before. Better a smaller farm with no loan than a bigger one the bank owns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anja and Filip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're keeping the farm but it'll look different, more machines, fewer sheep maybe. Anja would ask if she can drive the robot. Probably yes.

She'd push for a **shared machinery** scheme through the farmers' group.
think: Pavel's **surveying reports** could be AI work by 2028, hitting steady income.

do: **Sell** the bottom twenty hectares to Alan to clear the loan.
**Invest** in a shared robot scheme with three neighbours.
**Help** Pavel move into outdoor site inspections.
feel: **Worried but busy**, on the phone every night.
S2.quote: A small farm like mine can't buy the robot in 2031, but the big farm down the road can, and then sell lamb cheaper than me.
fieldNote: Her fear is **competition**, not losing a job: scale wins once robots arrive.
Ready to **sell land** to be debt-free, a hard but clear choice.

steps.text: Sell the bottom twenty hectares to Alan to clear the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if small farms work together. Same message: share the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to share a robot with my neighbour Alan before the big farms make us both look slow. I wouldn't need to sell land. Pavel would have three years to shift his work before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the shared robot fund with Alan and two others by 2028, a bit each year. I'd keep growing the lamb boxes and the cider. And I'd automate everything on the thinking side right away, that's already happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Alan agree to share a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alan would grumble for a year and then agree, because his knees are going. He's sixty-eight. He'll want it more than me by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the cider add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something robots and big farms can't copy easily: our name, our orchard. People pay for a story.

say: **Five years** is enough if small farms work together.
The message stays the same: **share the machines** between neighbouring farms.
think: She could **share a robot** with Alan before big farms pull ahead.
No need to **sell land**, and Pavel has time to shift.
do: **Start** a shared robot fund with Alan and two others by 2028.
**Automate** all thinking tasks on the farm right away.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to share a robot with my neighbour Alan before the big farms make us both look slow.
fieldNote: Five years removes the need to **sell land**.
Sees **Alan's knees** as the reason he'll join in.
Bets on a **local brand** that big farms can't copy.

steps.text: Start a shared robot fund with Alan and two neighbours by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case for farmers like me. A decade to adjust, buy kit and change what we grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to pay off the farm loan and buy the robots outright, without asking anyone's permission. By 2039 I'm fifty-six, and I'd hope to know the sheep as well as Alan does now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the loan, keep using AI for everything on the screen side, and buy robots when they're proven and cheaper. Maybe a robot weeder for the orchard first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that prices fall for everyone once the robots spread. Food gets cheaper, and so do my lambs. But that's a 2040 problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell new farmers starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the animals with your hands first, then let the machines do the rest. Don't do it the other way round like me.

fieldNote: Independence matters: buying robots **without permission** from banks or partners.
Only worry is **falling prices** once robots spread widely.
Advice to newcomers: **hands first**, machines second.

steps.text: Overpay the farm loan each year until it's cleared

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because small farms can't buy robots in three years and the big ones can. What would help is cheap loans or grants for neighbours to buy machines together, so it's not just the big operators who get them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Why people like me farm at all. I bought a farm at forty to work with my hands, and I'd use every machine going to keep it.
